codes.meaning: A `uniform` or `static const` of a `.dsp` is called `DreamPassWeight`. The name is the pipeline's weight in the view -- the largest weight of its activations, which is how a volume's fade reaches the effect -- and the runtime supplies it. The declaration is dropped. A buffer of that name is DSH4400.
codes.fix: Rename the declaration. The weight needs none: every pass receives it, a material as its scalar parameter `DreamPassWeight` and a `.usf` as `DP_Weight`, and `param Fade = DreamPassWeight * 0.5;` hands it on under another name, scaled.

codes.title: '{0}.Previous': a built-in texture keeps no history.
A material has no '{0}' pin; did you mean '{1}'? Attribute names are case-sensitive.
codes.meaning: `m.<Name>` names no material pin. The table comes from the engine, so the message can suggest a spelling that differs only in case — the usual cause, since 1.x matched these case-insensitively and 2.0 does not.
codes.fix: Use the exact spelling. `EmissiveColor`, `BaseColor`, `Roughness`, `Normal`, `WorldPositionOffset`, `FrontMaterial` and the rest keep their engine names; the 1.x short forms (`Emissive`, `AO`, `WPO`, `PDO`) are carried as aliases in the catalog.

codes.title: This Custom node declares no output called '{0}'; its outputs are '{1}'. An output is declared by 'AdditionalOutputs'.
codes.meaning:
Three shapes, one code — all say "this node's outputs need naming". The message lists the outputs the class has.

- `.Name` on a multi-output node names no output of that class.
- A multi-output node was used as a value without naming an output, and it is not the value the place wants. A node takes its **default** (first) output where that output's type is exactly the type wanted. A node whose outputs are all **channel views** of one value — `UE.VertexColor()`'s `RGB`, `R`, `G`, `B`, `A`, all cut from one `float4` — also stands for that whole value where exactly its type is wanted, so `float4 VC = UE.VertexColor();` binds as it did in 1.x (when the default output leads the value, as `RGB` does). A node whose outputs are different values — `UE.SceneTexture(...)`'s `Color`, `Size`, `InvSize` — has no whole to stand for: anything but its default output's exact type has to name an output.
- A swizzle on a node of channel views asked for channels that sit on different outputs (`UE.VertexColor().ga`: `G` and `A` are separate pins). A swizzle that one view publishes exactly is that view (`.a` is `A`), and a swizzle inside the default output is a swizzle of it (`.rg`); across views there is no one pin to read.
codes.fix: Name one of the listed outputs — `UE.SceneTexture(SceneTextureId = PostProcessInput0).Color`, `UE.VertexColor().A` — or read the channels one output at a time and combine them (`float2(UE.VertexColor().g, UE.VertexColor().a)`; two identical calls are one node). `dsc export-catalog` writes out every class with its pins and its outputs; an unnamed masked output is listed under the channels it keeps.

codes.title: The builtin catalog is empty, so no 'UE.' expression and no material attribute can be resolved; export it with 'dsc export-catalog'.
codes.meaning: The binder was given an empty builtin catalog, so no `UE.` node and no material pin can be resolved and everything that names one will also report. This is normal for a tool running outside the editor; inside a compile it means the catalog was not loaded.
codes.fix: Export the catalog with `dsc export-catalog` and point the tool at it. Nothing else in the file is affected — the symbol index is still produced.

codes.title: '{0}.{1}' is not a node; did you mean '{0}.{2}'? Node names are case-sensitive.
codes.meaning: `UE.X` / `Substrate.X` names no class this engine has. Node names are **case-sensitive**; a case-only match is suggested.
codes.fix: Correct the spelling, or reach the class by its engine name with `UE.Expression(Class = "MaterialExpressionX")`. `Substrate.` only resolves the Substrate table.

codes.title: '{0}.{1}' is a node and has to be called: write '{0}.{1}(...)'.
codes.meaning: `UE.X` was written without an argument list. A node is made by calling it, even when it takes nothing.
codes.fix: Add the parentheses: `UE.Time()`.

codes.title: '{0}' is not a material expression class this engine has.
codes.meaning: The `Class` argument does not name a material expression class. The class name is accepted with or without its `MaterialExpression` prefix and as a full `/Script/Engine.…` path.
codes.fix: Check the spelling against the exported catalog.

codes.title: '{0}.{1}' has no pin or property called '{2}'.
codes.meaning: A named argument to a reflected node matches neither an input pin nor a reflected property of that class. Pins are tried first, then properties; a case-only match on either is suggested.
codes.fix: Correct the name. A literal that should be written into the node rather than connected to it usually has a `Const`-prefixed property name — `ConstA` beside the `A` pin.

codes.title: {0} expects {1}, and this is {2}.
codes.meaning: A value does not fit the pin it feeds: the wrong width, or a kind the pin does not take (a number into a MaterialAttributes pin, a texture into a numeric one). Also raised for the coordinates and the mip level of a texture sample.
codes.fix: Match the pin's type — the message names it. A pin that does not constrain its width takes whatever arrives.

codes.title: '{0}' is not a value of '{1}' on '{2}'.
codes.meaning: The value of an enumerated property is not one of that enum's values. A case-only match is suggested.
codes.fix: Use one of the listed spellings, written without the enum's prefix (`SamplerType = Normal`, not `SAMPLERTYPE_Normal`).

codes.title: 'Substrate.' already names the node, so it takes no 'Class' argument.
codes.meaning: A `Class` argument was given to a `Substrate.` call. The `Substrate.` prefix already names the class.
codes.fix: Drop the `Class` argument, or write the call as `UE.Expression(Class = "…")` instead.

codes.title: 'Class' takes the expression class as a quoted string.
codes.meaning: The `Class` argument is not a literal the binder can read. It accepts a quoted string, a bare identifier and a dotted name.
codes.fix: Write `Class = "MaterialExpressionConstant3Vector"`.

codes.title: 'UE.Expression' reaches a node this language has no name for, so it needs 'Class = "MaterialExpressionName"'.
codes.meaning: `UE.Expression(...)` without `Class`. `Expression` is the escape hatch for a node the language has no name for, so the class is the one thing it cannot infer.
codes.fix: Add `Class = "MaterialExpressionName"`, or call the node by its short name.

codes.title: '{0}.{1}' leaves its required '{2}' pin unconnected; unless the node reads a default for it, the engine reports it when the material compiles.
codes.meaning: A pin the engine draws as required was left unconnected, and its literal twin was not set either. It is a warning, not an error: `required` only means the property has no `RequiredInput = "false"`. Most nodes do fail to compile with such a pin open, but some read a default instead (MakeMaterialAttributes, the per-level inputs of a switch, nodes of an engine fork that never set the metadata), and only the material compile knows. A class whose nodes show pins per setting has no statically required pin at all.
codes.fix: Connect the pin, or set its `Const...` property to a literal. If the node is meant to run with the pin open, nothing has to change; `dsc check -Shaders` compiles the material and reports a real `missing input`.

codes.title: '{0}.{1}' takes named arguments: write 'Pin = value'.
codes.meaning: A positional argument was given to a node that has no canonical argument order. Most reflected classes are named-only — the pin order an engine class happens to have is not a contract.
codes.fix: Name the argument: `Pin = value`.

codes.title: '{0}.{1}' takes {2} arguments in order; name the rest.
codes.meaning: More positional arguments than the node's canonical order defines.
codes.fix: Name the remaining ones.

codes.title: '{0}' is abstract and cannot be made into a node.
codes.meaning: The class is abstract and cannot be instantiated.
codes.fix: Use one of its concrete subclasses.

codes.title: '{0}' is an enumerated property; write one of its values, as in 'SamplerType = Normal'.
codes.meaning: A literal property was given something that is not a literal: an expression the binder cannot fold, or a word where a number was wanted. A property is written into the node when the graph is built, so its value has to exist at that moment.
codes.fix: Write a literal, or a `static const` expression that folds to one. A value that has to be computed belongs on a pin, not in a property.

codes.title: The first argument of a texture sample is the texture, and this is {0}.
codes.meaning: The first argument of `Texture2DSample` is not a texture.
codes.fix: Pass the texture — a `uniform Texture2D`, or a texture parameter of the function.

codes.title: The second argument of 'Texture2DSample' is the sampler, and this is {0}.
codes.meaning: The second argument of `Texture2DSample` is not a sampler.
codes.fix: Pass `<TextureName>Sampler`, the sampler the translator pairs with the texture, or use the shorter `Tex.Sample(UV)`, which takes it from the texture itself.

codes.title: Expected 'OutputIndex' to be a whole number of zero or more, found '{0}'.
codes.meaning: `OutputIndex` selects an output of a 1.x call by position, and its value is not a whole number from 0 up.
codes.fix: Write `OutputIndex = 1`, or name the output: `Output = "Alpha"`.

codes.title: Expected 'Output' to name an output with a quoted name or an identifier, found '{0}'.
codes.meaning: `Output` selects an output of a 1.x call by name, and its value is neither a quoted string nor an identifier.
codes.fix: Write `Output = "RGB"`.

codes.title: Expected either 'Output' or 'OutputIndex' on this call, found both.
codes.meaning: One 1.x call carries both `Output` and `OutputIndex`. They are two ways of choosing one output.
codes.fix: Keep one of them.

codes.title: Expected an output selector only on a call that has outputs, found one on the constructor '{0}'.
codes.meaning: An output selector (`Output` / `OutputIndex`) stands on a constructor such as `float3(...)`, which has no outputs.
codes.fix: Remove the selector, or take the component with a swizzle.

codes.title: '{0}' takes no positional argument here; 1.x ignored it, so it is dropped.
codes.meaning: A 1.x call spelling was given an argument it does not read: a positional argument where the spelling takes named ones only, or a named argument that is none of its own. 1.x skipped both without a word, so the node was built without that value; the front end drops it too and says so.
codes.fix: Name the argument the way the spelling reads it (`Pin = value`), or delete it.

codes.title: Expected 'UE.SceneTexture' to take exactly one argument, 'Id = ...', found {0} argument(s).
codes.meaning: The 1.x shorthand `UE.SceneTexture(Id = ...)` takes its scene texture id and nothing else.
codes.fix: Write `UE.SceneTexture(Id = PPI_SceneColor)`; any other property of the node needs `UE.Expression(Class = "SceneTexture", ...)`.

codes.title: Expected 'SampleTexture2D' to take exactly two positional arguments, a texture and coordinates, found {0} argument(s).
codes.meaning: The 1.x shorthand `SampleTexture2D(Texture, UV)` takes exactly a texture and coordinates.
codes.fix: Pass both and nothing else; for a mip level or derivatives use `UE.Expression(Class = "TextureSample", ...)`.

codes.title: Expected 'UE.StaticSwitchParameter' to name its parameter with 'Name = "..."', found no name.
codes.meaning: `UE.StaticSwitchParameter(...)` has no `Name`. The name is the parameter an instance overrides, and what makes two calls the same switch.
codes.fix: Add `Name = "Use Detail"`.

codes.title: Expected the static switch '{0}' to be called with a 'True = ...' and a 'False = ...' input, found at most one of them.
codes.meaning: A static switch is called without both of its sides. The node chooses between its `True` and `False` inputs; with one of them missing there is nothing to choose.
codes.fix: Pass `True = ...` and `False = ...`.

codes.title: Expected every argument of the parameter call '{0}' to name an input pin, found a positional argument.
codes.meaning: A property that is a parameter node (a `TextureSampleParameter2D`, a `StaticSwitchParameter`, ...) is called with a positional argument. Such a call is the node with its pins wired, and pins go by name.
codes.fix: Name each argument: `MyTex(Coordinates = uv)`.

codes.title: Expected a name after '::', found {0}.
codes.meaning: `Namespace::` is not followed by a function name.
codes.fix: Write `N::F(...)`.

codes.title: Expected 'OutputType' of a Custom expression to be float1 to float4 or MaterialAttributes, found '{0}'.
codes.meaning: The `OutputType` of a `UE.Expression(Class = "Custom", ...)` call is not a type a Custom node can return.
codes.fix: Use `float1` .. `float4` (or `float` .. `float4`), or `MaterialAttributes`.

codes.title: Expected 'Default' of 'UE.StaticSwitchParameter' to be true or false, found '{0}'.
codes.meaning: `Default` of a `UE.StaticSwitchParameter(...)` call is not `true` or `false`.
codes.fix: Write `Default = true`.

codes.title: Expected 'SortPriority' of 'UE.StaticSwitchParameter' to be a whole number, found '{0}'.
codes.meaning: `SortPriority` of a `UE.StaticSwitchParameter(...)` call is not a whole number.
codes.fix: Write an integer.

codes.title: Expected the parameter call '{0}' to take only its inputs, found an output selector.
codes.meaning: A call to a parameter-node property carries `Output` / `OutputIndex`. Such a call is rewritten into the node with its pins wired, and the selector has nowhere to go.
codes.fix: Select the output after the call with a member: `MyTex(Coordinates = uv).rgb`.

codes.title: '{0}' matches '{1}' only in case; a 1.x source is read ignoring case, so this is '{1}', and a '.dss' needs the exact spelling.
codes.meaning: Rule L19. A name in a 1.x source matches a declaration only when case is ignored. 1.x compared most names ignoring case, so the source builds; a `.dss` is case-sensitive.
codes.fix: Spell the name the way it is declared. `dsc migrate` does this for every such name.

codes.title: '{0}' matches the engine name '{1}' only in case; 1.x matched engine names ignoring case, so this is '{1}', and a '.dss' needs the exact spelling.
codes.meaning: Rule L19, for engine names: a `UE.` class, a pin, a property or an output matches only when case is ignored. 1.x looked these up ignoring case.
codes.fix: Use the engine's spelling, which the message shows. `dsc migrate` writes it.

codes.title: '{0}' is the GLSL spelling of '{1}'; a 1.x source may use it and it is read as '{1}', and a '.dss' writes '{1}'.
codes.meaning: Rule L2. A GLSL function or type spelling is used in a 1.x source (`mix`, `fract`, `mod`, `vec3`). 1.x rewrote them; a `.dss` takes HLSL only.
codes.fix: Write the HLSL name the message gives. `dsc migrate` does.

codes.title: '{0}' is the 1.x name of the '{1}' space of '{2}'; a '.dss' writes '{1}'.
codes.meaning: Rule L12. An enum value is written the engine's way (`PPI_SceneColor`, `TRANSFORM_Tangent`, `SAMPLERTYPE_Color`) or with its `Enum::` scope. 1.x matched enumerators loosely -- prefix, scope and case aside -- and this front end resolves the same value; a `.dss` takes the short form the catalog lists. The second message is a transform space by a name only 1.x had (`AbsoluteWorld`, `CameraRelativeWorld`, `FirstPerson`, `Particle`, `InstanceParticle`), which the front end writes as the engine's -- see [Transform builtins](../builtins/transform.md).
codes.fix: Write the value as the message spells it.

codes.title: '{0}.{1}' leaves its required '{2}' pin unconnected, which 1.x allowed and the engine reports when the material compiles.
codes.meaning: Rule L13. A `UE.` node is built in a 1.x body with a pin open that the engine draws as required. 1.x checked this only for a few of its hand-registered builtins (the `Input` of a transform was one), and many such sources compile because the node reads a default. In a `.dss` the same thing is DSH5219, also a warning.
codes.fix: Wire the pin if the material fails to compile with 'missing input'; otherwise nothing has to change.

codes.title: '{0}' has no output to select, and this call selects '{1}'.
codes.meaning: A 1.x call selects an output (`Output = ...`, `OutputIndex = ...`, or a receiver passed last) on something that has none: a helper with no result, or a call that is no node and no function.
codes.fix: Remove the selector, or call something that has the output.

codes.title: An output is selected by a whole number the compiler knows, and this index is computed.
codes.meaning: `node[k]` reads output `k` of a node, and `k` is not a constant the compiler can evaluate. Which wire is connected cannot depend on a run-time value.
codes.fix: Use a literal index, or name the output.

codes.title: This Custom node declares {0} output(s), counted from 0, and this selects output {1}.
codes.meaning: An output index is past the outputs the node or function declares. Outputs count from 0; a Custom node has its return value at 0 and its additional outputs after it.
codes.fix: Use an index inside the range, or name the output.

codes.title: '{0}' is not declared, and as in 1.x it is declared here as a local of type {1} receiving '{2}' of '{3}'.
codes.meaning: Rule L5. A 1.x statement call passes a receiver (`F(a, Out)`) that is declared nowhere. 1.x declared it on the spot with the type of the output it receives, and the front end does the same.
codes.fix: Nothing has to change. `dsc migrate` writes the declaration out.

codes.title: '{0}' becomes an input of the custom node, which carries a number or a texture, and this argument is {1}.
codes.meaning: An argument of a `Custom` node call is a value a Custom node input cannot carry: a material, a Substrate value, a sampler. A Custom input takes a number or a texture.
codes.fix: Pass the components the code needs (`m.BaseColor`), not the whole material.

codes.title: '{0}.{1}' has {2} input pin(s), counted from 0, and this argument connects pin {3}.
codes.meaning: `Pin[k] = value` names an input pin by its engine index, and the class has fewer pins than that.
codes.fix: Use an index the class has, or name the pin.

codes.title: 'Pin[{0}] = ...' connects a node's input pin by its engine index, and only a 'UE.' or 'Substrate.' node call has one; pass this argument by name or by position.
codes.meaning: `Pin[k] = value` is used on a call that is no `UE.` / `Substrate.` node: a user function, an intrinsic, a constructor. Only a reflected node has engine pin indices.
codes.fix: Pass the argument by name or by position.

codes.title: '{0}' has more than one output and is read as its first, '{1}', which is what 1.x did; a '.dss' names the output.
codes.meaning: Rule L3c. A node with several outputs is used as a value in a 1.x body without saying which output. 1.x read the first one; so does this front end, and it says which that is. It does so where the catalog gives that output no width, and wherever the node is passed straight to a pin (`UE.TransformPosition(UE.WorldPosition(), ...)` takes `XYZ`), because 1.x connected it there as it was and the pin took what it uses *(2.0.0 – 2.1.0 refused the pin case with `DSH5201`)*.
codes.fix: Nothing has to change. A `.dss` names the output (`UE.ScreenPosition().ViewportUV`), and `dsc migrate` writes it.

codes.title: '{0}.{1}' has no 'DefaultValue', so the default written for this parameter is dropped, as 1.x dropped it.
codes.meaning: A 1.x property is a parameter node without a `DefaultValue` property (a collection parameter, for one) and has a default written after `=`. 1.x dropped it.
codes.fix: Remove the default; set the value where the node takes it (the collection asset).

codes.title: {0} expects {1}, and this is {2}: its leading components are taken, which is what 1.x did; a '.dss' writes the swizzle.
codes.meaning: Rule L22. A value is wider than the place it goes -- a `float4` parameter assigned to a `vec3` variable, passed as a `float3` argument -- and 1.x cut it down to its leading components without a word. Only a wider value into a narrower place: two operands of different widths are still an error (DSH4226).
codes.fix: Nothing has to change. Writing the swizzle (`Tint.rgb`) says what is meant, and `dsc migrate` writes it.

codes.title: The asset of this block and a function this file can call are both named '{0}', which 1.x kept apart; the block is declared as '{1}', and a '.dss' writes that name.
codes.meaning: Rule L23. A block builds an asset named like a function this file can call (a `ShaderFunction(Name = ".../MF_X")` next to a `Function MF_X`). 1.x kept assets and functions in two tables, so both existed; 2.0 has one name table, and the block's function is declared as `<Name>_Asset` while the asset keeps its name.
codes.fix: Nothing has to change. The migrated file declares the export under the new identifier with a `/// @name` for the asset.

codes.title: '{0}.{1}' lists no pin called '{2}'; it is connected by that name once the node exists, because a node may name its pins after its properties.
codes.meaning: Rule L24. A named argument is not a pin or property the catalog lists for the class. The catalog is read off each class's default object, and some nodes name their pins after a property (MoonToonModifier shows other pins per modifier, TextureSample shows `CoordinatesDX` only under `MipValueMode = Derivative`, a Landscape layer blend calls its pins `Layer Grass` / `Height Rock` after its `Layers`). The pin is wired by that name on the node once it exists; if the node shows no such pin, the build fails there (DSH8212). In a `.dss` this applies only to classes the catalog flags as naming their pins per node; elsewhere an unknown name is DSH5213. In a `.dss`, such a pin fixes no width either: a numeric output is as wide as the widest value on one, and a `material` on one makes the output a `material`.
codes.fix: Nothing to do if the name is what the node shows. The pin's own property name (`ChannelW`) always resolves and does not need the lookup.

codes.title: '{0}' is not declared, and as in 1.x this assignment declares it, as a local of type {1}.
codes.meaning: Rule L26. `x = value;` in a 1.x body assigns to a name declared nowhere. 1.x declared the variable there, with the type of the value.
codes.fix: Nothing has to change; `dsc migrate` writes `T x = value;`. In a `.dss` an undeclared name is an error.

codes.title: A Substrate value has no compound assignment; write 'S = S + T' (Substrate.Add) or 'S = S * w' (Substrate.Weight).
codes.meaning: An operator that Substrate values do not have. They take `A + B` (`Substrate.Add`), `A * w` and `w * A` with a scalar (`Substrate.Weight`) and `lerp(A, B, t)` (`Substrate.HorizontalMix`), and nothing else. Three messages: another operator (`A - B`, `A * B`, `-A`); a `lerp` whose first two arguments are not both Substrate values or both numbers; a compound assignment (`A += B`), which would make the declaration of `A` mean two nodes.
codes.fix: Write the node you mean: `Substrate.Layer(Top, Base, Thickness)` for layering, `lerp` for mixing, and `A = A + B;` instead of `A += B;`.

codes.title: 'Substrate.{0}' is a node Unreal Engine has from {1} on; this engine does not have it.
codes.meaning: A piece of Substrate sugar needs a node this engine does not have. Three messages: a `Substrate.X(...)` call whose node exists from a later Unreal Engine version on (the message names the version); an operator, a run-time branch or a virtual argument that stands for such a node; and the same on an engine that has no Substrate nodes at all (before 5.4).
codes.fix: Build against an engine that has the node, or write what the sugar stands for with the nodes this engine has -- for a run-time branch, a `/// @static` condition or a `lerp`. Guard the code with `#if DS_ENGINE_MINOR >= ...` when one source has to build on both.

codes.title: '{0}.{1}': '{2}' and '{3}' parameterize the same pins; give one of them.
codes.meaning: Two arguments parameterize the same pins. `BaseColor` / `Metallic` / `Specular` become `DiffuseAlbedo` and `F0` through a conversion node, so giving `DiffuseAlbedo` or `F0` as well leaves two values for one pin; `IOR` computes `F0`, so it conflicts with `F0` and with the metalness arguments; `Haziness` becomes `SecondRoughness` and `SecondRoughnessWeight`; `Transmittance` becomes `SSSMFP`. The same rule holds for a value built member by member, where the two writes are on different lines.
codes.fix: Keep one parameterization: either the legacy one (`BaseColor`, `Metallic`, `Specular`) or the pins (`DiffuseAlbedo`, `F0`).

codes.title: '{0}.Thickness' is how deep 'Transmittance' is measured, and '{0}' was given no 'Transmittance' before this use.
codes.meaning: A virtual argument came without the one it is measured against. `Haziness` converts the BSDF's own `Roughness` into a second lobe, so it needs `Roughness`; `Thickness` is how deep `Transmittance` is measured, so it needs `Transmittance`. For a value built member by member the question is asked when the value is first used: the companion has to be written by then.
codes.fix: Give the companion -- `Roughness` with `Haziness`, `Transmittance` with `Thickness` -- in the same call, or before the first use of the value.

codes.title: '{0}' has been assigned a whole Substrate value since it was declared, and that value has no members; build a new value, or write the members before the assignment.
codes.meaning: A member of a Substrate value is written after the value stopped being a builder. Two messages: the value has been used already (passed, assigned, returned, combined with another), which made its node, and a later write could not change that node; or the local has been assigned a whole Substrate value since it was declared, and a finished value has no members.
codes.fix: Write every member before the first use of the value. To vary a value after using it, build a second one.

codes.title: A member of the Substrate value '{0}' cannot be written inside an 'if': that would be one node in two versions. Build two values and choose between them.
codes.meaning: A member of a Substrate value is written inside an `if` that the value's declaration is outside of. The value is one node, and a pin connected on one path only would be that node in two versions. (A builder declared inside the arm is that arm's own, and may be written there.)
codes.fix: Compute the pin's value with the branch and write it once -- `S.Roughness = wet ? 0.1 : 0.8;` -- or build two values and choose between them.

codes.title: '{0}' builds a '{1}.{2}', which has no pin called '{3}'.
codes.meaning: A member access on a Substrate value being built does not work out. Three messages: the node the value builds has no pin or virtual argument of that name; the member is read before anything wrote it -- a member reads back what was written to it, and the node's own default is not a value in the graph; the member is the left side of `*=`, `+=`, `++` and their kin before anything wrote it.
codes.fix: Check the pin's name against the node (`dsc export-catalog`, or hover in the editor extension), and assign a member before reading it.

codes.title: 'UE.{0}' needs {1}, and this engine's node catalog does not have it.
codes.meaning: `UE.DreamPassOutput`, `UE.DreamPassBuffer` or the engine's `UE.UserSceneTexture` is called, and the node catalog this file is bound against does not have the class. The two Custom Pass nodes are listed on Unreal Engine 5.8 and later only: below it their classes still exist, but they compile to a material error, so the catalog leaves them out and the call is refused here rather than built into a material that cannot compile. `UE.UserSceneTexture` came with 5.6. A catalog exported with `dsc export-catalog` from such an engine gives the same answer.
codes.fix:
Build with an engine that has the node. A source that has to build on an older engine as well guards the call:

```hlsl
#if DS_ENGINE_MAJOR > 5 || (DS_ENGINE_MAJOR == 5 && DS_ENGINE_MINOR >= 8)
    UE.DreamPassOutput(Output0 = float4(1, 0, 0, 0));
#endif
```

codes.title: Material '{0}' asks for the new material translator ('bEnableNewHLSLGenerator = true'), and uses {1} (line {2}), which only the classic translator compiles; remove the setting.
codes.meaning: The material sets `bEnableNewHLSLGenerator = true` in its `#pragma material`, and its graph holds a `UE.DreamPassOutput` or `UE.DreamPassBuffer` node, written in the entry or in a helper the entry inlines. Neither node implements the new material translator, so the material would not compile. The message stands on the setting and gives the line of the first node.
codes.fix: Remove `bEnableNewHLSLGenerator` from the `#pragma material`, or set it to `false`. A material that needs the new translator cannot use the Custom Pass nodes.

codes.title: UE.DreamPassOutput does nothing in '{0}', a {1}: the engine compiles custom outputs from a material's own graph only, and only there does the node give the material its DreamPass shader tag. A material using '{0}' writes no pass outputs, and a mesh pass in 'Mode = Own' does not draw it; write UE.DreamPassOutput in the material itself.
codes.meaning: `UE.DreamPassOutput` is called in a material function, a material layer or a layer blend (an `export`ed function, or one marked `@layer` / `@layerblend`), directly or through a helper it inlines. The engine compiles custom outputs from a material's own graph only, so in a function the node writes nothing and does not give the calling material the DreamPass shader tag: a material that has the node only there is not drawn by a mesh pass in `Mode = Own`, and has no outputs for a mesh pass that names it as its `Material` (DSH7340). It is a warning because the function itself still builds.
codes.fix: Write the node in the material: in its entry, or in a plain helper the entry calls, which is inlined into the material's graph. Let the function return the values the outputs need, and pass them to `UE.DreamPassOutput` there.

codes.title: Material '{0}' gets a second UE.DreamPassOutput node here (the first is on line {1}), and a material compiles one custom output of a class; write all four outputs in one call. A call inside a loop, or in a helper called twice, makes more than one node.
codes.meaning: One material's graph would get two `UE.DreamPassOutput` nodes, and a material compiles one custom output of a class -- the engine would fail it. Two calls make two nodes. So does one call inside a loop, which unrolls into more than one, and one call in a helper the material calls twice (or from a loop), because a helper is inlined at every call. The message stands at the second node and gives the line of the first.

codes.title: UE.DreamPassBuffer names no Pipeline: write the name of the '.dsp' (Pipeline = "CP_Highlight") or the pipeline asset's path.
codes.meaning: `UE.DreamPassBuffer` does not say which pipeline it reads. Two messages: the call has no `Pipeline` argument, or an empty one; or `Pipeline` is written as a path -- `/Game/...`, `Path(...)`, a pasted `Class'/Game/...'` reference -- that does not resolve to an object path, and the message quotes why (a malformed `Path(...)`, a pasted reference of another class than a pipeline).
codes.fix:
Name the pipeline by the name of the `.dsp` that builds it, or by the pipeline asset's path:

```hlsl
float Glow = UE.DreamPassBuffer(Pipeline = "CP_Highlight", Buffer = "Blurred").r;
```

codes.title: No pipeline named '{0}' is built by a .dsp under '{1}'; write the pipeline asset's path, or check the name.
codes.meaning: `Pipeline` is a bare name, and no `.dsp` under the source root of this `.dss` builds a pipeline of that name. A bare name is looked up the way a `.dsi`'s `Parent` is: among the products of the same source root. A pipeline is named after its `.dsp` file.
codes.fix: Check the name against the `.dsp`'s file name. A pipeline under another source root, or one no `.dsp` builds, is named by its asset path: `Pipeline = "/Game/Passes/CP_Highlight"`.

codes.title: '{0}' names more than one pipeline under this source root ({1}); write the pipeline asset's path instead.
codes.meaning: `Pipeline` is a bare name, and more than one `.dsp` under this source root builds a pipeline of that name -- two files of one name in different folders. The message lists them.
codes.fix: Write the asset path of the one you mean, or rename one of the files.

codes.title: The pipeline '{0}' names nothing: no pipeline asset exists at '{1}', and no .dsp under the source roots builds it.
codes.meaning: The reference resolved to an object path where no pipeline asset exists, and no `.dsp` under the source roots builds the pipeline, so nothing can stand in for it. Usually the path names nothing: a typo, or an asset that was moved or renamed. A pipeline that a `.dsp` builds is not this error, even when the `.dsp` does not compile: a `dsc check`, which builds nothing, reads that `.dsp` in place of the missing asset, and one that fails is DSH5319, with its first error.
codes.fix: Correct the path, or name the pipeline by its `.dsp`'s bare name.

codes.title: The pipeline '{0}' comes from '{1}', which failed to compile, so the buffer this material reads cannot be checked. {2}
codes.meaning:
The pipeline comes from a `.dsp` that does not compile, so the buffer this material reads cannot be checked. Two messages, one per kind of run:

- a run that builds assets found the pipeline asset missing or older than its `.dsp`, built the `.dsp` first (DSH5320 says so), and that compile failed (`... which failed to compile ...`);
- a run that builds nothing -- a `dsc check` -- found no pipeline asset and read the `.dsp` in its place, and the `.dsp` does not compile (`... which does not compile ...`).

The message ends with the `.dsp`'s first error. When that error is DSH8333, the pipeline and this material need each other: the cycle DSH5325 describes, met from the material's side.
codes.fix: Fix the `.dsp` -- compile it on its own to see all its diagnostics -- then compile the material again. For DSH8333, change the read as DSH5325 says.

codes.title: The pipeline '{0}' was missing or older than its source, so '{1}' was compiled first.
codes.meaning: The pipeline this material reads was missing or older than its `.dsp`, so the compile built the `.dsp` first, the way a `.dsi`'s parent is built first. Only a run that builds assets does this; a `dsc check` leaves the pipeline as it is. Said before that compile runs; DSH5319 follows if it fails.
codes.fix: Nothing to fix.

codes.title: The node's own rule refuses the buffer -- in the words the material editor would use.
codes.meaning:
The node's own rule refuses the buffer -- in the words the material editor would use. With the pipeline asset there, the message says which:

- `Buffer` names a built-in texture (`SceneColor`, `CustomDepth`, ...), which lives in the frame's render graph only; nothing copies it out.
- The pipeline has no buffer of that name.
- The buffer is not exported.
- The buffer is `Depth32` or an integer format, which a material cannot sample.
- The buffer is exported and the asset has no render target for it.

A built-in texture is this error from both paths: when the pipeline has not been built yet and its `.dsp` is read in its place (a `dsc check` on a fresh checkout), it is refused before any buffer is looked up, in the same words, so a check says what a build says. The `.dsp` path's other refusals have codes of their own (DSH5322, DSH5323).

A `dsc check` reads the pipeline asset as it is on disk, so a buffer added or exported in the `.dsp` since its last compile is not there yet.
codes.fix: Name a buffer the pipeline declares with `Export = true`, in a float or normalized format. When the `.dsp` already says so, compile it -- that also makes a missing render target -- then the material.

codes.title: The pipeline '{0}' declares no buffer '{1}'.
codes.meaning: The pipeline has not been built yet, so its `.dsp` was read in its place (a `dsc check` on a fresh checkout), and the buffer does not fit. Two messages: the `.dsp` declares no buffer of that name -- compared ignoring case, as the built asset compares it -- or the buffer is not `Export = true`. A built-in texture does not end here: it is refused first, as DSH5321, in the node's own words.
codes.fix:
Name a buffer the `.dsp` declares, and declare it with `Export = true`:

```hlsl
buffer Blurred : R8(Scale = 0.5, Export = true);
```

codes.title: Buffer '{1}' of the pipeline '{0}' is {2}, which a material cannot sample. Export a float or normalized buffer instead.
codes.meaning: The pipeline has not been built yet, its `.dsp` was read in its place, and the exported buffer is `Depth32`, `R32U` or `RG32U`. A material declares the texture as a float `Texture2D` and samples it with a filtering sampler, which none of these formats allows. This is a backstop: the `.dsp` itself refuses such an export first (DSH7355, DSH7321), and a `.dsp` that does not compile is not read here (DSH5319).
codes.fix: Export a float or normalized format -- `R8`, `RG16F`, `R32F` -- instead.

codes.title: UE.DreamPassBuffer names no Buffer of '{0}': write the exported buffer's name (Buffer = "Blurred").
codes.meaning: `UE.DreamPassBuffer` names its pipeline and no buffer of it: `Buffer` is missing, empty or `None`.
codes.fix: Write the exported buffer's name: `Buffer = "Blurred"`.

codes.title: The pipeline '{0}' needs this material to be built -- it is one of its pass materials, or the material of a pipeline that one needs -- so this material cannot read its exported buffer: the two can be built in no order. Inside its own pipeline a pass binds the buffer with 'read' -- a fullscreen material reads it as a UserSceneTexture input -- rather than the exported copy; a mesh pass's material cannot read its own pipeline's buffers.
codes.meaning: This material reads, through `UE.DreamPassBuffer`, an exported buffer of a pipeline that needs the material built: the pipeline draws it as one of its pass materials, or one of its pass materials reads a pipeline that draws it. The two can be built in no order -- compiled first, the material has no pipeline asset to read; compiled second, the pipeline has no material to draw (DSH4406) -- so the pair can never bootstrap, and the read is refused. It is raised when the material is compiled or read from inside the pipeline's compile, which builds a missing or stale pass material first; the `.dsp` then reports its material as failing (DSH8331). Met from the material's side, the same cycle is the `.dsp`'s DSH8333, which the material reports as DSH5319.

codes.title: '{0}' is a {1}, not a DreamShader pass pipeline.
codes.meaning: `Pipeline` names an asset that exists and is not a pass pipeline: a material, a texture -- often the render target an exported buffer becomes, `CP_Highlight_Blurred`, picked instead of the pipeline `CP_Highlight`. The message names its class.
codes.fix: Point `Pipeline` at the pipeline asset, or at its `.dsp`'s bare name, and name the buffer with `Buffer`.

codes.title: '{0}' is a second material entry; '{1}' above it is already the entry, and one file makes one material.
codes.meaning: Two exported functions in one file have the signature `void (inout material)`. That signature *is* the declaration of the material entry, so a file with two of them describes two materials. The message names both.
codes.fix: Keep one; move the other to its own file, or drop `export` to make it a helper that takes a material — an internal function with that signature is not an entry.

codes.title: '{0}' is exported from a file whose entry is '{1}'; a file makes a material or it makes functions, not both. Move it to its own file, or drop 'export' to make it a helper.
codes.meaning: A file has a material entry **and** exported functions, layers or layer blends. One file makes one kind of product. A 1.x `.dsm` is the exception: its `Shader` and the `ShaderFunction` and layer blocks beside it are all built, as 1.x built them *(2.0.0 – 2.1.0 refused them here too)* -- and that is why `dsc migrate` cannot turn such a file into one `.dss`.
codes.fix: Move the functions to their own file and `#include` it, or drop `export` so they become helpers that are inlined into the material.

codes.title: 'extern {0}' has nothing to bind to; add '/// @asset /Game/.../MF_Name' above it.
codes.meaning: An `extern` prototype has no `/// @asset` above it, so there is nothing for it to bind to.
codes.fix: Add `/// @asset /Game/.../MF_Name` naming the existing material function.

codes.title: '@layer' makes '{0}' a material layer asset, so it has to be 'export'.
codes.meaning: `@layer` or `@layerblend` on a function that is not `export`. Both directives name an asset the file produces, and only an exported function produces one.
codes.fix: Add `export`, or delete the directive.

codes.title: A '@layer' function is written 'export void {0}(inout material m)'.
codes.meaning: A `@layer` function does not have the signature `void Name(inout material m)`.
codes.fix: Write it with exactly that signature. A layer takes the material it is applied to and modifies it in place.

codes.title: A '@layerblend' function is written 'export void {0}(material Base, material Top, ..., inout material Result)': at least one 'material' input and a final 'inout material'.
codes.meaning: A `@layerblend` function does not have the shape `void Name(material A, material B, …, inout material Result)`: at least one `material` input, every other parameter an input, and a final `inout material`.
codes.fix: Reorder the parameters so the result comes last and is `inout material`.

codes.title: '{0}' is a builtin operation and cannot be redeclared; rename the function.
codes.meaning: A function is declared with the name of a builtin operation (`dot`, `lerp`, `saturate`, …, and the GLSL spellings the language rejects). There is no overloading, so the two would be ambiguous at every call site.
codes.fix: Rename the function.

codes.title: '{0}' is a {1} asset, not a function this file may call.
codes.meaning: A call to the material entry, a `@layer` or a `@layerblend`. Those are assets, not functions this file may call — a layer is applied by the material that uses it.
codes.fix: Factor the shared code into a helper and call that from both.

codes.title: '{0}' has no body; a prototype has to be 'extern' and carry '/// @asset'.
codes.meaning: A function has no body and is not `extern`. Normally the parser catches this first (DSH3208); this is the semantic backstop for a tree that reached the binder some other way.
codes.fix: Give it a body, or declare it `extern` with `/// @asset`.

codes.title: '{0}' is '@custom', so '{1}' becomes an input pin of a Custom node, and a Custom node cannot take a material; pass the fields it needs instead.
codes.meaning: A `/// @custom` function takes a `material` as an input (`material m` or `inout material m`). A `@custom` body becomes a Custom node, whose inputs are pins the material translator types, and there is no MaterialAttributes input type for one.
codes.fix: Pass the fields the body needs — `float3 BaseColor, float Roughness` — and write the results back at the call site. A `material` **return** and an `out material` parameter stay legal: a Custom node may produce attributes even though it cannot consume them.

codes.title: '{0}' is an 'out' parameter of '{1}' but the body never assigns it, so a caller would read a value nothing produced. Assign it before the function returns, or remove the parameter.
codes.meaning: A function declares an `out` parameter and its body never writes it — not as a whole, not a swizzle, element or field of it, and not by passing it to another call's `out` / `inout` parameter. A caller reading that output would get a value nothing produced; in the graph it is an unconnected pin. A write on one branch only is enough to satisfy this check: it is "never", not "not on every path".
codes.fix: Assign the parameter before the function returns, or remove it. Functions with an opaque body (`/// @custom`, 1.x `Function`) and `extern` prototypes are not checked; their bodies are not DreamShaderLang statements.

codes.title: '{0}' calls itself, and an inlined function has no stack to recurse on; rewrite it as a loop with a constant trip count, or as a '/// @custom' function.
codes.meaning: An inlined function calls itself, directly or through others. Inlining has no stack: a call is replaced by the callee's body, so a recursive call would expand forever.
codes.fix: Rewrite the recursion as a loop with a constant trip count (which unrolls), or move it into a `/// @custom` function, where HLSL's own rules apply -- though HLSL has no recursion either, so the loop is usually the real answer. A mutual recursion between two helpers reports at whichever call closes the cycle; both functions are named in the message across the two reports.

codes.title: Resolving the defaults of '{0}' would go {1} calls deep, past the limit of {2}; pass explicit values or flatten the default call chain.
codes.meaning: Inlining went deeper than `MaxInlineDepth` (32 by default) without recursing. A chain of thirty-two helpers each calling the next is legal and just very deep; the limit is there so a pathological file fails with a message rather than exhausting memory.
codes.fix: Flatten the call chain, or turn one of the middle functions into an `export`ed material function, which becomes its own asset and a single `FunctionCall` node rather than more inlined nodes. Raising the limit is a pipeline option, not a source one.

codes.title: '{0}' is an '{1}' parameter of {2}, so the argument has to be something that can be assigned to; this expression cannot.
codes.meaning: An argument passed to an `out` or `inout` parameter is not something that can be assigned to. The parameter writes back into the caller when the call finishes, so the argument has to name a variable, a field, a material attribute or a swizzle of one -- not a computed value.
codes.fix: Put the result in a local and pass that: `float3 Value; Compute(Value); Use(Value);`. Passing a literal, a call's result or an arithmetic expression to an `out` parameter cannot work.

codes.title: '{0}' is this file's material entry and is called by the engine, not by the shader.
codes.meaning: Either a call to this file's material entry -- the `void (inout material)` function the engine calls, not the shader -- or a call to a function that has no body to inline: a prototype that is neither `extern` with `/// @asset` nor `/// @custom`.
codes.fix: For the entry, call the helper the entry calls, not the entry itself. For a body-less function, give it a body, mark it `extern` and point `/// @asset` at the material function asset it stands for, or mark it `/// @custom` and write its HLSL.

codes.title: The default value of '{0}' in '{1}' depends on itself; pass an explicit value for a parameter in the cycle.
codes.meaning: An omitted parameter's default depends on itself (directly, through other defaults, or through another call with omitted arguments), or reads an input that has no value. The same code also reports a Custom function's default expression writing an `out` parameter: that output has no input pin through which the graph-computed initial value could reach the HLSL body.
codes.fix: Pass an explicit value to break the dependency cycle, or give the referenced input a usable default. For a Custom output, pass its initial value through a separate input and assign the output in the HLSL body. Ordinary helper defaults may initialize `out` parameters; those values are carried into the helper body and copied back normally.

codes.title: '{0}' has no verbatim HLSL body, so it cannot become a custom node; only a '/// @custom' function can.
codes.meaning: `BuildDreamShaderCustomNodeCode` was called for a function index that does not exist, or for a function the binder did not classify as `EBoundFunctionKind::Custom`, or — when a helper is reached through a call — for a `@custom` function whose body the parser did not capture verbatim (`FFunctionDecl::bOpaqueBody` is false, so `RawBody` is empty).
codes.fix: Inside a compile this is an internal error, not an authoring mistake: the IR builder decided to make a Custom node for something that is not a custom function, or the parser and the binder disagree about which bodies are opaque. Report it with the source file attached. From a tool that calls the entry point directly, pass the index of a function whose `///` block carries `@custom`.

codes.title: '{0}' declares '{1}' as 'inout', which a custom node cannot carry; split it into an 'in' parameter and an 'out' parameter.
codes.meaning: A `@custom` parameter is declared `inout`. A custom node carries its `out` parameters as *additional outputs*, which the engine already declares as `inout` parameters of the function it generates; an input pin of the same name would declare that name a second time, and the shader would not compile. There is no form of a custom node that both reads and writes one pin.

codes.title: '{0}' takes the material '{1}' as an input; a custom node cannot accept material attributes on a pin, so read the fields the body needs and pass them as floats.
codes.meaning: A `@custom` function takes `material` (material attributes) as an input. The engine's translator types every Custom-node input pin and has no case for material attributes — the shader compile ends with `Bad type MaterialAttributes for <node> input <pin>`. Material attributes are fine as a custom node's *output*; they are not accepted on the way in.

codes.title: '{0}' uses Substrate on '{1}'; a custom node has no Substrate pins, so build that part of the material out of reflected Substrate nodes.
codes.meaning: A `@custom` signature mentions `Substrate`. A custom node has no Substrate pins in any engine version; 1.x refused the same thing on a `Function`.
codes.fix: Build the Substrate part of the material out of reflected `Substrate.*` / `UE.*` nodes and keep the `@custom` function to the float maths around it.

codes.title: '{0}' returns a texture through '{1}'; a custom node output carries float1..4 or material attributes, never a texture object.
codes.meaning: A `@custom` function returns a texture or a sampler, or hands one back through an `out` parameter. A custom node's outputs are `float1`..`float4` or material attributes; there is no pin that carries a texture object, and HLSL will not return one from a function either.
codes.fix: Sample the texture inside the body and return the sampled value. A texture may be an *input*; it is the output direction that has no form.

codes.title: '{0}' declares '{1}' twice in the HLSL it generates; a texture parameter also claims '{1}Sampler', which the engine declares alongside it.
codes.meaning: Two parameters of one `@custom` function end up with the same name in the HLSL that is generated for it. The usual cause is the sampler pairing: a `Texture2D Tex` parameter also claims `TexSampler`, because that is the name the engine declares beside it, so a second parameter actually called `TexSampler` collides. Names are compared case-sensitively, as HLSL compares them.
codes.fix: Rename one of them. A `SamplerState` parameter is never paired automatically, so it is the one to rename when a texture and an explicit sampler meet.

codes.title: '{0}' returns void but its body uses 'return;'; a custom node always returns its first output, so give the function a return type or restructure the body.
codes.meaning: A `@custom` function declared `void` uses a bare `return;` in its body. The function the engine generates around that body always returns the node's first output, so a `return;` with no value does not compile — at any brace depth, not only at the top.
codes.fix: Give the function a return type and return a value, or restructure the body so the early exit becomes an `if`. A `void` `@custom` is legal — its node simply outputs 0 and does its work through `out` parameters — it just cannot `return`.

codes.title: '{0}' declares a return type but its body never returns a value; the node's first output will be 0.
codes.meaning: A `@custom` function declares a return type, but its body contains no `return` anywhere (the warning does not fire for a body that is a single bare expression, which is given its `return` automatically). The node's first output will be the constant 0.
codes.fix: Return the value the signature promises, or declare the function `void` and use `out` parameters if the body is only there for its side effects.

codes.title: '{0}' has an '#include' with an empty path; write the virtual shader path the header lives at, for example "/Engine/Private/Common.ush".
codes.meaning: A `#include` at the top of a `@custom` body has an empty path (`#include ""`). Leading includes are lifted onto the node's include list, and an empty entry would reach the shader compiler as `#include ""`.
codes.fix: Write the virtual shader path the header lives at — `/Engine/Private/Common.ush`, `/Plugin/DreamShader/DreamShaderBuiltins.ush`, `/Plugin/<Name>/...`. Only `#include` lines at the very top of a body (whitespace and comments may come before them) are hoisted; one that follows a statement stays in the body, where it lands inside a function and only works for macro headers.

codes.title: '{0}' differs from the function '{1}' only in case; HLSL is case-sensitive, so this call is left for the shader compiler. Did you mean '{1}'?
codes.meaning: A call inside a `@custom` body names something that differs from a function of this module only in case — `remap01(x)` where the module declares `Remap01`. DreamShaderLang 1.x matched function names case-insensitively; 2.0 bodies are HLSL, and HLSL is case-sensitive, so the call is left for the shader compiler to resolve.
codes.fix: Spell the name the way the function is declared. If the call is genuinely meant for a symbol from one of the body's own `#include`s and the collision is a coincidence, rename one of the two — there is no way to tell them apart at this level.

codes.title: The '@custom' functions {0} call each other in a cycle; HLSL has no recursion, so their bodies cannot be embedded in a custom node.
codes.meaning: Two or more `@custom` functions call each other, directly or through others. Their bodies are embedded into the calling node as members of one struct, and HLSL has no recursion, so there is no order that works. The message names the cycle.
codes.fix: Break the cycle: pull the shared part into a third `@custom` function that calls nobody, or move the recursion into a hand-written `.ush` header the body `#include`s (where the shader compiler will still refuse real recursion, but a bounded unrolled form can be written by hand).

codes.title: '{0}' is not a '@custom' function and cannot be called from the HLSL body of '{1}'; a custom node sees no graph values, so mark '{0}' '@custom' as well or move the call out of the body.
codes.meaning: A `@custom` body calls a function of this module that is not itself `@custom` — a helper, an `export`ed material function, or an `extern`. Those become graph nodes; a custom node's body is HLSL that the shader compiler sees long after the graph is built, and it has no way to reach a graph value.
codes.fix:
Mark the callee `/// @custom` too, so its body can be embedded alongside; or take the value as a parameter of the custom function and compute it in the graph:

```hlsl
/// @custom
float3 Shade(float3 Color, float Mask) { ... }   // Mask computed by the caller, in the graph
```

codes.title: '{0}' takes {1} argument(s) but this call passes {2}; a call that carries a texture cannot be matched up by position otherwise.
codes.meaning: A call to a `@custom` function that takes a texture passes the wrong number of arguments. The companion sampler has to be spliced in next to each texture argument, which means the arguments have to line up with the parameters by position; with the wrong count there is no way to know which argument is the texture.
codes.fix: Pass exactly one argument per parameter. A default value on a parameter does not let you leave it out here — the sampler pairing needs every position.

codes.title: The texture argument for '{0}' of '{1}' has to be a plain texture name, because the sampler that goes with it is named after it.
codes.meaning: The argument in a texture position of a call to a `@custom` function is not a plain name (`Pick(a, b)`, `bUseA ? A : B`, `Textures[i]`). The sampler that goes with a texture is named after the texture — `Tex` brings `TexSampler` — so the argument has to be a name for that to mean anything. 1.x built the sampler name by pasting `Sampler` onto whatever the argument's text was, which turned `a ? b : c` into `a ? b : cSampler`; 2.0 refuses instead of emitting that.
codes.fix: Assign the texture to a name first, or choose between textures in the graph and pass the chosen one in as a parameter of the outer custom function.

codes.title: '{0}' is 'selfcontained', so the '@custom' function '{1}' it calls is not embedded in its node; the call is left for the shader compiler to resolve out of this body's own includes.
codes.meaning: A `@custom selfcontained` body calls another `@custom` function of the module. A `selfcontained` body is taken exactly as written — nothing of the module is embedded into it — so the call is left for the shader compiler, which will only find the symbol if one of this body's own `#include`s defines it.
codes.fix: Drop `selfcontained` if the call is meant to be embedded (that is the default behaviour, and the closure is pulled in for you). Keep `selfcontained` if the symbol really comes from an included header, and rename the local `@custom` function so the two do not look like the same thing.

codes.title: '{0}' takes {1} argument(s) in the HLSL it becomes, but this call passes {2}.
codes.meaning: A `@custom` body calls another `@custom` function with a number of arguments the HLSL that function becomes does not take. HLSL has no default arguments and a `@custom` function no overloads, so the shader compiler would refuse the call; it is refused here instead, at the call. The count is of the HLSL function: a 1.x function that returns nothing returns its first `out` (rule L9), so a call of it passes every parameter but that one -- or every parameter, which is read as `r = F(a, o)`.
codes.fix: Pass one argument per parameter of the callee, `out` parameters included. A file `dsc migrate` wrote that fails here is a fault of the migration; say so.

codes.title: '{0}' returns nothing in the HLSL it becomes, so this call has no value to read; pass a variable for each of its 'out' parameters and read those.
codes.meaning: A `@custom` body reads the value of a call to a `@custom` function that returns nothing -- `x = F(a, o)`, `return F(a)`, `F(a) + 1`. Its HLSL is `void`, so there is no value. Under 1.x every such function returned its first `out` (rule L9), and a 1.x body read that; a `.dss` function is emitted as it is declared.
codes.fix: Pass a variable for each `out` parameter and read it after the call, or declare the function returning the value. `dsc migrate` makes a 1.x function return its first `out`; a `Namespace` function keeps its `out`s and a body of its file that read one calls an adapter that returns it.

codes.title: Expected a function name after '{0}', found '('.
codes.meaning: `Function` or `GraphFunction` (with its optional modifier and return type) is followed by `(` where the function's name should be.
codes.fix: Write `Function float3 MyFunction(in float3 value) { ... }`.

codes.title: Expected '[in|out] Type Name' in the parameter list of '{0}', found '{1}'.
codes.meaning: A parameter of a 1.x function is not `[in|out] Type Name`. 1.x parameters have no defaults and no metadata; those belong to the `Inputs` of a ShaderFunction.
codes.fix: Write each parameter as `in float3 color` or `out float result`.

codes.title: Expected 'in' or 'out' before the parameter '{0}' of '{1}', found '{2}'; a 1.x function has no 'inout'.
codes.meaning: A parameter of a 1.x function carries `inout`, or another word where `in` / `out` goes. 1.x functions had inputs and results, never a parameter that was both.
codes.fix: Split it into an `in` and an `out` parameter. A `.dss` function may use `inout`.

codes.title: Expected a parameter name other than '__return', which 1.x reserved, in '{0}'.
codes.meaning: A parameter is called `__return`. 1.x lowered a function's return value into an `out` parameter of that name, so the name is taken.
codes.fix: Rename the parameter.

codes.title: Expected either a return type or 'out' parameters on '{0}', found both.
codes.meaning: A 1.x function has a return type and `out` parameters. 1.x allowed one or the other: a returned value is the Custom node's output, and so is the first `out`.
codes.fix: Return the first result and keep no `out` parameter, or drop the return type and make every result an `out`.

codes.title: Expected '{0}' to return a value or to have at least one 'out' parameter, found neither.
codes.meaning: A 1.x function returns nothing and has no `out` parameter, so its Custom node would have no value for the graph to read.
codes.fix: Give it a return type or an `out` parameter.

codes.title: 'Inline' is the old spelling of 'SelfContained', and both read the same: the function's node embeds the functions it calls.
codes.meaning: `Function Inline` is used. In 1.x `Inline` is an exact synonym of `SelfContained`: the function's Custom node embeds the functions its body calls. 2.0 embeds them into every Custom node, so both spellings read the same as no modifier at all, and the function becomes a plain `@custom`. It never becomes `@custom selfcontained`, which in 2.0 means the opposite -- embed nothing (`DSH6264`). *(2.0.0 – 2.1.0 read both spellings as `@custom selfcontained`.)*
codes.fix: Drop the modifier, or write `SelfContained`; nothing changes either way.

codes.title: Expected a return type or a name after 'GraphFunction', found the modifier '{0}', which only a Function takes.
codes.meaning: `GraphFunction` is followed by `SelfContained` or `Inline`. Those modifiers belong to `Function`; a GraphFunction is always one Custom node per call.
codes.fix: Remove the modifier.

codes.title: Expected a value after 'return' in '{0}', which returns '{1}', found a bare 'return;'.
codes.meaning: A 1.x function with a return type contains a bare `return;`. 1.x lowered `return x;` into an assignment to its result, and a `return` without a value has nothing to assign.
codes.fix: Return a value on every path.

codes.title: Expected a 'Name = "..."' attribute with a name on 'Namespace', found none.
codes.meaning: `Namespace` has no `Name = "..."` attribute, or the name is not an identifier. The name becomes the prefix of every function in the block (`N::F`, flattened to `N_F`).
codes.fix: Write `Namespace(Name = "BL") { ... }`.

codes.title: Expected only Function and GraphFunction blocks inside the namespace '{0}', found {1}.
codes.meaning: A `Namespace` block holds something other than `Function` and `GraphFunction` blocks. A namespace groups HLSL functions and nothing else: no assets, no VirtualFunctions, no nested namespaces.
codes.fix: Move the other block out of the namespace.

codes.title: Expected a 'Name = "..."' attribute with a name on 'VirtualFunction', found none.
codes.meaning: `VirtualFunction` has no `Name = "..."` attribute. The name is what Graph code calls.
codes.fix: Add the name.

codes.title: Expected an 'Asset = Path(...)' option on the VirtualFunction '{0}', found none.
codes.meaning: A VirtualFunction has no `Asset = Path(...)` in its `Options`. The whole point of the block is to say which existing material function the name stands for.
codes.fix: Add `Options = { Asset = Path(Game, "Functions/MF_Example"); }`.

codes.title: Expected at least one output on the VirtualFunction '{0}', found none.
codes.meaning: A VirtualFunction declares no output. A call to it would be a node nothing can read.
codes.fix: Declare the outputs of the asset under `Outputs`, in the asset's order.

codes.title: Expected a ')' to close the 'UE.' call in the body of '{0}', found the end of the body.
codes.meaning: A `UE.` call in a verbatim body -- a 1.x GraphFunction, or a `/// @custom` function -- opens a parenthesis that the body never closes, so the call that is to be lifted into a node input has no end.
codes.fix: Close the call. If the text is not meant as a node call, it cannot start with `UE.` followed by a name and `(`.

codes.title: A 'Substrate.' call in the body of '{0}' is not lifted into a node, because no custom node input carries a Substrate value; it reaches the shader compiler as text.
codes.meaning: A verbatim body calls `Substrate.<Node>(...)`. `UE.` calls in such a body are lifted into inputs of the Custom node; a Substrate value cannot travel through a Custom node input, so the call is left where it is and the shader compiler will not know the name.
codes.fix: Build the Substrate node in a graph body and keep only numbers in the HLSL.

codes.title: Expected '(' to open the parameter list of '{0}', found {1}.
codes.meaning: A 1.x function's name is not followed by `(`, or its parameter list is not followed by the `{` that opens its body.
codes.fix: Write the parameter list, empty if need be, and the body: `Function float Pi() { return 3.14159; }`.

codes.title: '{0}' lifts a 'UE.' call out of its body that reads '{1}', which 1.x took from the caller's scope and 2.0 does not; pass '{1}' to '{0}' as a parameter.
codes.meaning: Rule L8. A `UE.` call lifted out of a GraphFunction body reads a variable of the CALLER. 1.x evaluated lifted calls in the caller's scope, so this worked by accident of naming; the lifted call is now bound in the function's own scope -- its parameters and the file's globals -- so that a function means the same thing wherever it is called.
codes.fix: Add a parameter for the value and pass it at the call.

codes.title: '{0}' lifts a 'UE.' call out of its body that reads '{1}', which is neither a parameter of '{0}' nor declared at file scope.
codes.meaning: A `UE.` call lifted out of a verbatim body reads a name that is neither one of the function's parameters nor declared at file scope. A lifted call is evaluated in the graph, outside the HLSL, so it cannot see a variable the body declares.
codes.fix: Pass the value in as a parameter, or compute it in the graph and hand the result to the function.

codes.title: '{0}' takes the 'UE.' calls lifted out of its body as inputs of its own custom node, so the HLSL body of '{1}' cannot call it; call it from a graph body instead.
codes.meaning: An HLSL body calls a function whose own body has `UE.` calls lifted out of it. Those calls are inputs of that function's OWN Custom node; embedded as a helper in another node's code it would have nobody to wire them.
codes.fix: Call the function from a graph body and pass its result in, or move the `UE.` calls out of it into parameters.

codes.title: '{0}' lifts the call behind its input '{1}' out of a place its body does not have, so its custom node's code cannot be built.
codes.meaning: A lifted call's recorded place lies outside the body text it belongs to. The front end records where each `UE.` call stands in the body and the code builder replaces that range by the input's name; the two disagree only when a declaration was altered between them. Internal error.
codes.fix: Report it with the source.

codes.title: '{0}' carries 'UE.' calls lifted out of its body, and only a '@custom' function with a verbatim body lifts calls into its node's inputs.
codes.meaning: A function that is not a `/// @custom` function with a verbatim body carries lifted calls, or a lifted call makes a value no Custom input carries (a material, a Substrate value). The first is an internal inconsistency; the second means the body calls a node whose result is not a number or a texture.
codes.fix: For the second case, build that node in a graph body instead of inside the HLSL.

codes.title: '{0}' reaches itself through the 'UE.' calls lifted out of its body, and each call makes a new custom node, so the graph would never end.
codes.meaning: A function reaches itself through a call lifted out of its body: the lifted `UE.` call's arguments call the function again. Each call of such a function is a new Custom node with its own lifted inputs, so the expansion would not end.
codes.fix: Break the cycle: compute the inner value in the graph and pass it in.

codes.title: '{0}' is not an attribute of a '{1}' block, and was ignored; the header takes Generate, Library and Description.
codes.meaning: A 1.x `Function` or `GraphFunction` header *(after 2.1.2)* names a key other than `Generate`, `Library` and `Description` -- usually a misspelling. The other 1.x blocks ignore an unknown key silently, as 1.x did; this header is new, so a typo is said. See [Packages ▸ Asset headers](../tools/packages.md#asset-headers).
codes.fix: Spell the key as one of the three, or remove it.

codes.title: '{0}' holds a placeholder other than '`{Name`}', the only one a Generate template has.
codes.meaning: A `Generate` value -- a 1.x function's own, or a `Namespace`'s template applied to a member -- still holds a `{...}` after `{Name}` was replaced. `{Name}` is the only placeholder a template has.
codes.fix: Write `{Name}` exactly (it is case-sensitive), or write the name out.

codes.title: Invalid boolean value '%s' for %s.
codes.meaning: A setting that is a bool was given something other than `true` / `false` (any case).
codes.fix: Write `true` or `false`.

codes.title: Setting path segment cannot be empty.
codes.meaning: A material setting key that is not one of the well-known ones (`BlendMode`, `ShadingModel`, `Domain`, ...) is read as a reflection path into `UMaterial`: property names separated by `.`, with `[index]` on a fixed-size array. This key has an empty segment: a leading or trailing `.`, or two in a row.
codes.fix: Remove the stray `.`.

codes.title: Invalid array setting segment '%s'.
codes.meaning: A material setting key that is not one of the well-known ones (`BlendMode`, `ShadingModel`, `Domain`, ...) is read as a reflection path into `UMaterial`: property names separated by `.`, with `[index]` on a fixed-size array. A segment of this key has a `[` without a property name in front of it, or without its `]`.
codes.fix: Write the segment as `Name[2]`.

codes.title: Invalid array index '%s' in setting segment '%s'.
codes.meaning: A material setting key that is not one of the well-known ones (`BlendMode`, `ShadingModel`, `Domain`, ...) is read as a reflection path into `UMaterial`: property names separated by `.`, with `[index]` on a fixed-size array. The text between `[` and `]` is not a whole number of zero or more.
codes.fix: Use a literal index: `Name[2]`.

codes.title: Invalid array setting segment '%s'.
codes.meaning: A material setting key that is not one of the well-known ones (`BlendMode`, `ShadingModel`, `Domain`, ...) is read as a reflection path into `UMaterial`: property names separated by `.`, with `[index]` on a fixed-size array. Something follows the `]` of a segment other than the next `.`.
codes.fix: Write one index per segment: `Name[2].Field`.

codes.title: Invalid material setting target.
codes.meaning: The settings were applied to no material. Internal error: the asset was not created before its settings were written.
codes.fix: Report it with the source; the first error of the same build usually names the real cause.

codes.title: Invalid material setting path '%s'.
codes.meaning: A material setting key that is not one of the well-known ones (`BlendMode`, `ShadingModel`, `Domain`, ...) is read as a reflection path into `UMaterial`: property names separated by `.`, with `[index]` on a fixed-size array. This key could not be split into segments at all (empty, or only dots).
codes.fix: Write the property name as the material's Details panel property is called in C++ (`TranslucencyLightingMode`, not its display name).

codes.title: Unsupported material setting '%s'.
codes.meaning: A material setting key that is not one of the well-known ones (`BlendMode`, `ShadingModel`, `Domain`, ...) is read as a reflection path into `UMaterial`: property names separated by `.`, with `[index]` on a fixed-size array. No property of that name exists on the material (or on the struct the path has reached). Display names do not count; neither do editor-only categories.
codes.fix: Look the property's C++ name up in `Material.h`. The keys with a meaning of their own are listed in `Docs/settings`.

codes.title: Setting '%s' is not an indexed array property.
codes.meaning: A setting key puts `[index]` on a property that is not a fixed-size array.
codes.fix: Remove the index.

codes.title: Array index %d is out of range for setting '%s' (max %d).
codes.meaning: A setting key indexes a fixed-size array past its end. The message gives the last valid index.
codes.fix: Use an index inside the array.

codes.title: Setting '%s' requires an explicit [index].
codes.meaning: A setting key names a fixed-size array without saying which element.
codes.fix: Add `[index]`.

codes.title: Setting path '%s' cannot continue through '%s'.
codes.meaning: A setting key continues with `.Field` after a property that is not a struct, so there is nothing to look `Field` up in.
codes.fix: End the path at that property, or fix the property name in front of the `.`.

codes.title: Invalid material setting path '%s'.
codes.meaning: A setting path ran out of segments without reaching a property. Internal backstop of the path walker.
codes.fix: Report it with the key that caused it.

codes.title: Failed to create a transient material for Settings validation.
codes.meaning: Settings are validated against a scratch material before anything is built, and that scratch object could not be created. This points at an engine in a bad state (out of memory, shutting down), not at the source.
codes.fix: Retry; if it persists, restart the editor.

codes.title: Invalid value '%s' for setting '%s'. %s
codes.meaning: The value of a reflected setting does not fit its property's type; the sentence after it says what the type expected (a bool, an integer, an enum value, an object path ...). Raised while the settings are validated, before any asset is touched.
codes.fix: Write the value in the form that sentence asks for. Enum values go by their short name (`TLM_Surface` or `Surface`).

codes.title: Invalid value '%s' for setting '%s'. %s
codes.meaning: Same as DSH7125, raised while the setting is applied to the real material -- reached only when validation passed and the asset then refused the value, which means the property differs between the scratch material and the asset's class.
codes.fix: Check the value against the property's type; report it if DSH7125 did not fire first.

codes.title: Unsupported BlendMode/RenderType '%s'.
codes.meaning: `BlendMode` (or its 1.x alias `RenderType`) is not a value of the engine's `EBlendMode`. Values are matched without the `BLEND_` prefix, ignoring case, spaces and underscores; hidden enum entries do not count.
codes.fix: Use `Opaque`, `Masked`, `Translucent`, `Additive`, `Modulate`, `AlphaComposite`, `AlphaHoldout`, or whatever else this engine's enum has.

codes.title: ShadingModel="Substrate" requires Unreal Engine 5.4 or newer.
codes.meaning: `ShadingModel = Substrate` is set on an engine older than 5.4, which has no Substrate front material.
codes.fix: Use a classic shading model there, or build with 5.4 or newer.

codes.title: Unsupported ShadingModel '%s'.
codes.meaning: `ShadingModel` is not a value of the engine's `EMaterialShadingModel` (matched without `MSM_`, ignoring case, spaces and underscores).
codes.fix: Use one of the engine's names without the `MSM_` prefix (`DefaultLit`, `Unlit`, `Subsurface`, `ClearCoat`, `TwoSidedFoliage`, `Hair`, `Cloth`, `Eye`, `SingleLayerWater`, `ThinTranslucent`, `Substrate`, ...); an engine fork may add its own.

codes.title: Unsupported MaterialDomain '%s'.
codes.meaning: `Domain` is not a value of the engine's `EMaterialDomain` (matched without `MD_`, ignoring case).
codes.fix: Use `Surface`, `DeferredDecal`, `LightFunction`, `Volume`, `PostProcess` or `UI`.

codes.title: Invalid reflected property target.
codes.meaning: A literal was to be written into a property that does not exist on the object. Internal error: the catalog listed a property the live class does not have.
codes.fix: Report it; re-exporting the catalog (`dsc export-catalog`) rules out a stale manifest.

codes.title: '%s' is not a valid boolean value for '%s'.
codes.meaning: A bool property of a node (or a bool setting) was given something other than `true` / `false`.
codes.fix: Write `true` or `false`.

codes.title: '%s' is not a valid integer value for '%s'.
codes.meaning: An integer property was given text that is not a whole number.
codes.fix: Write an integer, without a decimal point.

codes.title: '%s' is not a valid unsigned integer value for '%s'.
codes.meaning: An unsigned integer property was given a negative number or text that is no number.
codes.fix: Write a whole number of zero or more.

codes.title: '%s' is not a valid numeric value for '%s'.
codes.meaning: A float property was given text that is not a number.
codes.fix: Write a number. A vector property takes `(X=..,Y=..,Z=..)` in the engine's own text form, not an HLSL constructor.

codes.title: '%s' is not a valid numeric value for '%s'.
codes.meaning: A double property was given text that is not a number.
codes.fix: Write a number.

codes.title: Object property '%s' expects Path(...) or an absolute Unreal object path.
codes.meaning: An object property (a texture, a function, a collection) was given text that is neither `Path(Root, "...")` nor an absolute object path such as `/Game/Textures/T_Noise`.
codes.fix: Write the asset as `Path(Game, "Textures/T_Noise")` or as its object path.

codes.title: Failed to load asset '%s' for '%s'.
codes.meaning: The asset an object property names could not be loaded: the path is wrong, the asset was moved, or its plugin is not mounted in this project.
codes.fix: Copy the reference from the Content Browser (*Copy Reference*) and paste it in; check that the plugin owning the asset is enabled.

codes.title: Asset '%s' is not compatible with '%s'. Expected '%s'.
codes.meaning: The asset loaded, and it is not of the class the property takes: a Texture2D where a TextureCube is expected, a material where a function is.
codes.fix: Point the property at an asset of the class the message names.

codes.title: '%s' is not a valid enum value for '%s'.
codes.meaning: An enum property (an `FEnumProperty`) was given a name that is not one of the enum's values. Values are matched with and without the enum's prefix, ignoring case.
codes.fix: Use one of the values the builtin catalog lists for that property (`dsc export-catalog`).

codes.title: '%s' is not a valid enum value for '%s'.
codes.meaning: Same as DSH7140, for the older `TEnumAsByte` kind of enum property.
codes.fix: Use one of the enum's values.

codes.title: '%s' is not a valid byte value for '%s'.
codes.meaning: A byte property that is not an enum was given text that is not a number from 0 to 255.
codes.fix: Write a number from 0 to 255.

codes.title: Property '%s' on '%s' is not a supported literal type yet.
